claim: The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is necessary for inferring value in tests of model-based reasoning, including in sensory preconditioning.
source: The orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) is necessary for inferring value in tests of model-based reasoning, including in sensory preconditioning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Neural correlates of broader associative structure exist in OFC during the initial phase of sensory preconditioning.
source: We recently reported neural correlates of such broader associative structure in OFC during the initial phase of sensory preconditioning (Sadacca et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim references a specific prior study by the authors.

claim: Inhibition of OFC during cue-cue learning abolished value inference during the probe test.
source: We found that inhibition of OFC during cue-cue learning abolished value inference during the probe test, inference subsequently shown in control rats to be sensitive to devaluation of the expected reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study supported by experimental data.

claim: Value inference in control rats during the probe test is sensitive to devaluation of the expected reward.
source: We found that inhibition of OFC during cue-cue learning abolished value inference during the probe test, inference subsequently shown in control rats to be sensitive to devaluation of the expected reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the devaluation experiment.

claim: OFC must be online during cue-cue learning for proper value inference.
source: These results demonstrate that OFC must be online during cue-cue learning, consistent with the argument that the correlates previously observed are not simply downstream readouts of sensory processing and instead contribute to building the associative model supporting later behavior.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing effects of OFC inhibition.

claim: The neural correlates previously observed in OFC are not simply downstream readouts of sensory processing.
source: These results demonstrate that OFC must be online during cue-cue learning, consistent with the argument that the correlates previously observed are not simply downstream readouts of sensory processing and instead contribute to building the associative model supporting later behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: OFC neural correlates contribute to building the associative model supporting later behavior.
source: These results demonstrate that OFC must be online during cue-cue learning, consistent with the argument that the correlates previously observed are not simply downstream readouts of sensory processing and instead contribute to building the associative model supporting later behavior.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Humans and laboratory animals cannot infer value in several situations when OFC function is impaired.
source: This ability relies on a circuit involving the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), as evidenced by the finding that humans and laboratory animals cannot infer value in several situations when OFC function is impaired (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; McDannald et al., 2005; Takahashi et al., 2009; West et al., 2011; Gremel and Costa, 2013; Reber et al., 2017; Howard et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Model-based reasoning can be isolated in sensory preconditioning.
source: Model-based reasoning can be isolated in sensory preconditioning (Brogden, 1939).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In sensory preconditioning, presentation of the never-reward-paired preconditioned stimulus will produce a strong food-approach response after one stimulus is paired with food.
source: If one of these stimuli is thereafter paired with a biologically meaningful stimulus (e.g. food), presentation of the never-reward-paired preconditioned stimulus will produce a strong food-approach response.
evidence: This describes the established behavioral phenomenon of sensory preconditioning.

claim: The response to the preconditioned cue cannot be explained by model-free mechanisms.
source: Because the preconditioned cue itself was never reinforced, this response to the preconditioned cue cannot be explained by model-free mechanisms.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the definition of model-free learning.

claim: Preconditioned responding reflects the ability to infer value on-the-fly using knowledge about associative structure.
source: Preconditioned responding is reflective of the ability of subjects to infer value on-the-fly using knowledge about the associative structure of the information acquired during preconditioning.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established understanding of sensory preconditioning.

claim: Lateral OFC activity is necessary for inferring the value of never-reinforced sensory stimuli in the probe test at the end of sensory preconditioning.
source: Previous work from our lab has shown that the lateral OFC activity is necessary for inferring the value of never-reinforced sensory stimuli in the probe test at the end of sensory preconditioning (Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work from the authors' lab.

claim: Neural activity in the OFC reflects not only value predictions in the final probe test, but also tracks acquisition of sensory-sensory associations in the initial phase of training.
source: Interestingly, subsequent single-unit recording showed that neural activity in the OFC reflects not only the value predictions in the final probe test, but also tracks acquisition of the sensory-sensory associations in the initial phase of training (Sadacca et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior single-unit recording study.

claim: OFC has a wider role in building associative models, independent of encoding overt biological significance or value.
source: This result suggested a wider role for OFC in building associative models, independent of encoding of overt biological significance or value, the role often ascribed to this region (Kringelbach, 2005; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Levy and Glimcher, 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior recording results, contrasted with cited literature.

claim: Single-unit recording is correlative and cannot demonstrate that OFC activity is necessary for proper acquisition of sensory-sensory associations during preconditioning.
source: Of course, single-unit recording is correlative and cannot demonstrate that OFC activity is necessary for proper acquisition of the sensory-sensory associations during preconditioning.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of correlative methods, based on general scientific knowledge.

claim: The correlates observed in OFC could simply reflect activity in primary sensory or other cortical areas that are necessary in the first phase.
source: The correlates could simply reflect activity in primary sensory (Engineer et al., 2008; Garrido et al., 2009; Headley and Weinberger, 2015) or other cortical areas that are necessary in the first phase (Port et al., 1987; Robinson et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2014; Fournier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: If OFC correlates simply reflect downstream processing, then interference with OFC during preconditioning should not affect responding to the preconditioned cue during the probe test.
source: If this is the case, then interference with processing in OFC during preconditioning should not affect responding to the preconditioned cue during the probe test.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on a hypothetical scenario.

claim: If OFC representations contribute to building the task model, then interference with OFC during preconditioning should affect probe test responding.
source: On the other hand, if the representations of the sensory-sensory associations formed in OFC in the initial phase contribute to building the model of the task used to infer value and drive responding in the probe test, then interference with processing in OFC during preconditioning should affect probe test responding, either directly impairing normal responding to the preconditioned cue, if responding in our task is entirely model-based as we have suggested (Jones et al., 2012; Sadacca et al., 2018), or by making any responding insensitive to devaluation of the predicted food reward, if responding in the probe is partly maintained by transfer of cached value to the cue during conditioning (Doll and Daw, 2016).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on a hypothetical scenario, supported by citations.

claim: Interfering with processing in OFC during the preconditioning phase completely abolished responding to the preconditioned cue in the probe test after conditioning.
source: We found that interfering with processing in OFC during the preconditioning phase completely abolished responding to the preconditioned cue in the probe test after conditioning, responding that in controls was subsequently disrupted by devaluation of the expected food reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Responding to the preconditioned cue in controls was disrupted by devaluation of the expected food reward.
source: We found that interfering with processing in OFC during the preconditioning phase completely abolished responding to the preconditioned cue in the probe test after conditioning, responding that in controls was subsequently disrupted by devaluation of the expected food reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The NpHR experimental group received AAV5 containing halorhodopsin (NpHR) linked to a CamKIIα promoter.
source: One group, the NpHR experimental group (N = 21), received AAV5 containing halorhodopsin (NpHR) linked to a CamKIIα promoter.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: NpHR is a light gated chloride pump that induces neuronal hyperpolarization to allow real-time neuronal inactivation.
source: NpHR is a light gated chloride pump that induces neuronal hyperpolarization to allow real-time neuronal inactivation (Gradinaru et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the optogenetic tool, supported by citation.

claim: The eYFP control group received the same virus but without the opsin.
source: The other group of rats, the eYFP control group (N = 22), received the same virus but without the opsin.
evidence: This describes the control condition in the experimental design.

claim: Both viruses contained eYFP for histological verification of successful transfection.
source: Both viruses contained eYFP for histological verification of successful transfection.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods.

claim: All rats had fiberoptic probes implanted bilaterally overlying the injection site to allow light delivery.
source: All rats also had fiberoptic probes implanted bilaterally overlying the injection site to allow light delivery.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure used.

claim: Responding to the food cup during preconditioning was negligible, and there were no differences between cues or groups.
source: No reward was presented, so responding to the food cup during this phase was negligible, and there were no differences between cues or groups (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed no main effects of cue (F(3,123)=0.43, p=0.73) or group (F(1,41)=1.99, p=0.17) and no group x cue interaction (F(3,123)=0.86, p=0.46) during preconditioning.
source: A two-way ANOVA with cue as a within subjects factor and group as a between subjects factor revealed no main effects of cue (F(3,123)=0.43, p=0.73) or group (F(1,41)=1.99, p=0.17) and no group x cue interaction (F(3,123)=0.86, p=0.46).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Rats developed a conditioned response to B with training, responding more at the food cup during cue B than during cue D.
source: As expected, rats developed a conditioned response to B with training, responding more at the food cup during cue B than during cue D, and there was no difference between groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: There was no difference between groups in conditioned responding during the conditioning phase.
source: As expected, rats developed a conditioned response to B with training, responding more at the food cup during cue B than during cue D, and there was no difference between groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 2B.

claim: A three-way mixed-design ANOVA revealed significant main effects of cue (F(1,41)=143.00, p<0.0001) and session (F(5,205)=36.23, p<0.0001), and a significant session x cue interaction (F(5,205)=9.76, p<0.0001) during conditioning.
source: A three-way mixed-design (cue, session within subjects factors; group between subjects factor) ANOVA revealed significant main effects of cue (F(1,41)=143.00, p<0.0001) and session (F(5,205)=36.23, p<0.0001), and a significant session x cue interaction (F(5,205)=9.76, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There were no main effects of, nor any interactions with, group during conditioning.
source: Critically, there were no main effects of, nor any interactions with, group (main: F(1,41)=0.02, p=0.90; session x group: F(5,205)=1.72, p=0.13; group x cue interaction: F(1,41)=0.53, p=0.47).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Control rats responded more to A than C during the probe test.
source: We found that control rats responded more to A than C, and NpHR rats did not (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figures 2C-D.

claim: NpHR rats did not respond more to A than C during the probe test.
source: We found that control rats responded more to A than C, and NpHR rats did not (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figures 2C-D.

claim: A two-way mixed-design ANOVA revealed no main effects of cue (F(1,41)=1.33, p=0.26) or group (F(1,41)=0.00, p=0.99) during the probe test.
source: A two-way mixed-design ANOVA revealed no main effects of cue (F(1,41)=1.33, p=0.26) or group (F(1,41)=0.00, p=0.99).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was a significant cue x group interaction (F(1,41)=4.57, p=0.04) during the probe test.
source: There was a significant cue x group interaction (F(1,41)=4.57, p=0.04); ergo, the effect of cue during the probe test (A-C) did depend on group (eYFP control – NpHR OFC inhibition).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The effect of cue during the probe test (A-C) did depend on group (eYFP control – NpHR OFC inhibition).
source: There was a significant cue x group interaction (F(1,41)=4.57, p=0.04); ergo, the effect of cue during the probe test (A-C) did depend on group (eYFP control – NpHR OFC inhibition).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis.

claim: Posthoc comparisons revealed responding to A was significantly higher than C in controls (p=0.046).
source: Posthoc comparisons revealed responding to A was significantly higher than C in controls (p=0.046), but not in NpHR rats (p=0.75).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Posthoc comparisons revealed responding to A was not significantly higher than C in NpHR rats (p=0.75).
source: Posthoc comparisons revealed responding to A was significantly higher than C in controls (p=0.046), but not in NpHR rats (p=0.75).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: A subset of the eYFP rats (n = 13) were split into two groups (paired and unpaired) with equal responding to A and C.
source: To confirm the associative basis of responding to the preconditioned cue observed in controls, a subset of the eYFP rats (n = 13) were split into two groups (paired and unpaired) with equal responding to A and C (no main effect of group (F(1,11)=0.06, p=0.81) or group x cue interaction (F(1,11)=2.60, p=0.13)).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the devaluation test.

claim: All rats consumed all pellets during the first free exposure session.
source: All rats consumed all pellets during the first free exposure session.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: The paired group demonstrated a conditioned taste aversion, consuming significantly fewer pellets than in the first test (t(5) = 4.95, p=0.001).
source: Subsequently, during the second free exposure session, the paired group demonstrated a conditioned taste aversion, consuming significantly fewer pellets than in the first test (t(5) = 4.95, p=0.001, second exposure mean = 2.25 g, range = 0.6–3.0 g)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Responding extinguished quickly in both groups during the devaluation probe, however it was much higher in the unpaired group on the initial trials.
source: On probe, responding extinguished quickly in both groups, however it was much higher in the unpaired group on the initial trials (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of trial block (F(2,22)=4.91, p=0.02) and significant trial block x group interaction (F(2,22)=4.58, p=0.02) during the devaluation probe.
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of trial block (F(2,22)=4.91, p=0.02) and significant trial block x group interaction (F(2,22)=4.58, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Post hoc comparisons revealed responding was significantly higher to A in the unpaired group than the paired group during the first trial block (p=0.02).
source: Post hoc comparisons revealed responding was significantly higher to A in the unpaired group than the paired group during the first trial block (p=0.02; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the experimental data, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The change in responding was accompanied by reduced consumption of the outcome by rats in the paired group (t(11) = 4.95, p=0.0004).
source: This change in responding was accompanied by reduced consumption of the outcome by rats in the paired group (t(11) = 4.95, p=0.0004; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: The OFC is generally thought to contribute to behavior where there are changes in, or computations of, value.
source: While the OFC is generally thought to contribute to behavior where there are changes in, or computations of, value (Gallagher et al., 1999; Kringelbach, 2005; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Schoenbaum et al., 2011), our lab recently showed that neural activity in lateral OFC can also track the development of valueless sensory-sensory associative information in a sensory preconditioning task (Sadacca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neural activity in lateral OFC can track the development of valueless sensory-sensory associative information in a sensory preconditioning task.
source: While the OFC is generally thought to contribute to behavior where there are changes in, or computations of, value (Gallagher et al., 1999; Kringelbach, 2005; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Schoenbaum et al., 2011), our lab recently showed that neural activity in lateral OFC can also track the development of valueless sensory-sensory associative information in a sensory preconditioning task (Sadacca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Performance in the final phase of sensory preconditioning is sensitive to OFC manipulations in both rats and humans.
source: While performance in the final phase of this task is ultimately sensitive to OFC manipulations in both rats (Jones et al., 2012) and humans (Wang et al., 2020b), the development of neural correlates of neutral sensory associations in the initial phase of training suggested that OFC might not be restricted to encoding information once clear biological significance is established and instead could be more widely involved in representing structure among features of the environment, with value being just one of these features.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: OFC might be more widely involved in representing structure among features of the environment, with value being just one of these features.
source: While performance in the final phase of this task is ultimately sensitive to OFC manipulations in both rats (Jones et al., 2012) and humans (Wang et al., 2020b), the development of neural correlates of neutral sensory associations in the initial phase of training suggested that OFC might not be restricted to encoding information once clear biological significance is established and instead could be more widely involved in representing structure among features of the environment, with value being just one of these features.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from prior observations.

claim: Optogenetically-inactivating the OFC during the initial phase of preconditioning disrupted performance in the final phase of the task.
source: Here we tested this question by optogenetically-inactivating the OFC during the initial phase of preconditioning, when correlates were previously observed, and we found that this manipulation also disrupted performance in the final phase of the task.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The associative correlates observed during preconditioning are not simply downstream reflections of sensory or other cortical processing.
source: These findings are consistent with the argument that the associative correlates we observed during preconditioning in our prior study are not simply downstream reflections of sensory or other cortical processing and instead must contribute to the construction of the model used to guide responding in the final probe test.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The associative correlates must contribute to the construction of the model used to guide responding in the final probe test.
source: These findings are consistent with the argument that the associative correlates we observed during preconditioning in our prior study are not simply downstream reflections of sensory or other cortical processing and instead must contribute to the construction of the model used to guide responding in the final probe test.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: OFC represents not only value, but also features of the environment such as trial type, sequence, direction, and goal location.
source: These data are also in accord with the findings that OFC represents not only value, but also features of the environment such as trial type (Lopatina et al., 2017), sequence (Zhou et al., 2019), direction, and goal location (Feierstein et al., 2006; Mainen and Kepecs, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Generalization or failure to treat cues differently would be the final common outcome of disrupting the detailed encoding of their identities and different associative relationships to reward.
source: In considering this possibility, we would first note that generalization or failure to treat these cues differently would be to some extent the final common outcome of disrupting the more detailed encoding of their identities and different associative relationships to reward that we argue is affected.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between mechanisms.

claim: Generalization as a primary cause is unlikely given the low overall levels of responding to preconditioned cues during the probe, relative to responses to the reward-paired cue.
source: However we believe that generalization as a primary cause is unlikely given the low overall levels of responding to these cues during the probe, relative to responses to the reward-paired cue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: There is no evidence from other studies that the OFC is necessary for discriminating the sensory properties of cues.
source: There is also no evidence from other studies that the OFC is necessary for discriminating the sensory properties of cues; rats without OFC or in whom the OFC is inactivated perform well in a number of settings that require them to distinguish different cues to guide responding (Schoenbaum et al., 2002; Boulougouris et al., 2007; Takahashi et al., 2009; Jones et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: OFC was inhibited only during cue presentation, precisely when single unit correlates of cue-cue encoding were previously observed.
source: We inhibited OFC only during cue presentation, precisely when we previously observed single unit correlates of cue-cue encoding; our design did not include control conditions in which similar inhibition was done before or after the cues or during the intertrial intervals.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The design did not include control conditions in which similar inhibition was done before or after the cues or during the intertrial intervals.
source: We inhibited OFC only during cue presentation, precisely when we previously observed single unit correlates of cue-cue encoding; our design did not include control conditions in which similar inhibition was done before or after the cues or during the intertrial intervals.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: OFC must be online at the time the neural correlates were observed.
source: Thus, while we can conclude that OFC must be online at the time the neural correlates were observed, we cannot conclude that it does not need to be online at any other time during the first phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: We cannot conclude that OFC does not need to be online at any other time during the first phase.
source: Thus, while we can conclude that OFC must be online at the time the neural correlates were observed, we cannot conclude that it does not need to be online at any other time during the first phase.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in what can be concluded from the experiment.

claim: OFC can be inactivated briefly between trials without affecting OFC-dependent learning and behavior.
source: Although OFC can be inactivated briefly between trials without affecting OFC-dependent learning and behavior (Takahashi et al., 2013), we would not be surprised if processing outside the strictly defined cue period – say immediately before or after – were also necessary for normal learning.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Processing outside the strictly defined cue period might also be necessary for normal learning.
source: Although OFC can be inactivated briefly between trials without affecting OFC-dependent learning and behavior (Takahashi et al., 2013), we would not be surprised if processing outside the strictly defined cue period – say immediately before or after – were also necessary for normal learning.
evidence: This is speculation about what might be found in future experiments.

claim: Simply delivering light during the cue period is not sufficient to produce the observed effects.
source: While we know from our control group, that simply delivering light during the cue period is not sufficient, perhaps inhibiting OFC neurons during this period distracts the rats, because it is rewarding or punishing or for some other reason.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control group data.

claim: There was no evidence that OFC inhibition impacted learning and responding to cues in the later periods of the task.
source: If this were the case, then we would have expected to see an impact of this on learning and responding to these cues in the later periods of the task. We did not see any evidence of this.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Brief periods of OFC inhibition often have minimal or no effects on ongoing behavior.
source: Further we know from a number of prior studies that brief periods of OFC inhibition, similar to that employed here, often have minimal or no effects on ongoing behavior (Takahashi et al., 2013; Gardner et al., 2017; Gardner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Brief OFC inhibition is not, by itself, rewarding, painful or otherwise distracting.
source: These results suggest this is not, by itself, rewarding, painful or otherwise distracting.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior research.

claim: Lateral OFC inactivation is not sufficient to produce state-dependent learning.
source: Finally, it has been shown that lateral OFC inactivation is not sufficient to produce state-dependent learning, which provides very strong evidence that it does not create a tangible experience in and of itself (Panayi and Killcross, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: All rats received food cup approach shaping prior to preconditioning.
source: A final consideration is that all rats received food cup approach shaping prior to preconditioning.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Food cup approach shaping may change the salience of the conditioning chamber context and cause increased attention to the cues during preconditioning.
source: It is possible that this changes the salience of the conditioning chamber context and causes increased attention to the cues during preconditioning, which may facilitate learning.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: OFC contributes to risk, uncertainty and salience processing.
source: This idea would be consistent with results showing correlates of risk (O'Neill and Schultz, 2010; Ogawa et al., 2013), uncertainty (van Duuren et al., 2009) and salience (Ogawa et al., 2013) in OFC neurons, as well as the finding that OFC value coding is attentionally gated (McGinty et al., 2016) and active in auditory oddball task (Nguyen and Lin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: OFC value coding is attentionally gated.
source: This idea would be consistent with results showing correlates of risk (O'Neill and Schultz, 2010; Ogawa et al., 2013), uncertainty (van Duuren et al., 2009) and salience (Ogawa et al., 2013) in OFC neurons, as well as the finding that OFC value coding is attentionally gated (McGinty et al., 2016) and active in auditory oddball task (Nguyen and Lin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: OFC is active in auditory oddball task.
source: This idea would be consistent with results showing correlates of risk (O'Neill and Schultz, 2010; Ogawa et al., 2013), uncertainty (van Duuren et al., 2009) and salience (Ogawa et al., 2013) in OFC neurons, as well as the finding that OFC value coding is attentionally gated (McGinty et al., 2016) and active in auditory oddball task (Nguyen and Lin, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The role OFC plays in supporting salience is secondary to the associative learning role that OFC supports.
source: However, while it is possible that inactivating OFC affected learning of the sensory-sensory associations by interfering with a primary role for OFC in supporting the context or even cue salience, it seems more parsimonious to us to propose that the role OFC plays in supporting salience is secondary to the associative learning role that OFC clearly supports.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: Attentional models link cue salience to associative strength – changes in cue associative strength drive changes in salience.
source: This idea is consistent with attentional models, both old and new, that link cue salience to associative strength – changes in cue associative strength drive changes in salience (Mackintosh, 1975; Pearce and Hall, 1980; Haselgrove et al., 2010; Esber and Haselgrove, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical models.

claim: OFC is not the only area that is necessary for value-neutral sensory learning.
source: Of course, we do not intend to suggest that OFC is the only area that is necessary for this sort of value-neutral sensory learning. This is surely not the case.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the broader literature.

claim: Interfering with hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, and perirhinal cortex impairs the acquisition of sensory-sensory associations.
source: Indeed even when preconditioning is the readout, we know that interfering with several cortical areas including hippocampus (Port et al., 1987), retrosplenial cortex (Robinson et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2014; Fournier et al., 2020), and perirhinal cortex (Holmes et al., 2013; Wong et al., 2019) seems to impair the acquisition of sensory-sensory associations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most cortical and subcortical areas encode variables relevant to predicting biologically-relevant outcomes.
source: While most cortical and subcortical areas encode variables relevant to predicting biologically-relevant outcomes (Milad and Quirk, 2002; Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Kennerley et al., 2011; Cai and Padoa-Schioppa, 2012; Burgos-Robles et al., 2013; Giustino et al., 2016; Giustino et al., 2019; Halladay et al., 2020), few studies look at whether the same areas track incidental sensory-sensory associations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Few studies look at whether cortical and subcortical areas track incidental sensory-sensory associations.
source: While most cortical and subcortical areas encode variables relevant to predicting biologically-relevant outcomes (Milad and Quirk, 2002; Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Kennerley et al., 2011; Cai and Padoa-Schioppa, 2012; Burgos-Robles et al., 2013; Giustino et al., 2016; Giustino et al., 2019; Halladay et al., 2020), few studies look at whether the same areas track incidental sensory-sensory associations.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the literature.

claim: Other cortical areas (e.g. prelimbic, infralimbic, cingulate, retrosplenial) will likely also exhibit correlates of incidental sensory-sensory pairings, like OFC.
source: This account would predict that other cortical areas (e.g. prelimbic, infralimbic, cingulate, retrosplenial) will likely also exhibit correlates of incidental sensory-sensory pairings, like OFC, yet unique single unit responses would not be apparent until the probe test, when subjects must infer specific information about the preconditioned cues based on new information acquired during conditioning.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the current findings.

claim: fMRI correlates of cue-cue learning were observed in precentral gyrus, middle occipital gyrus, insula, and hippocampus in a human sensory preconditioning task.
source: Indeed, fMRI correlates of cue-cue learning were observed in precentral gyrus, middle occipital gyrus, insula, and hippocampus in a human sensory preconditioning task (Wang et al., 2020a), and single unit correlates also exist in nucleus accumbens (Cerri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Single unit correlates of cue-cue learning exist in nucleus accumbens.
